goal: Implement authentication for admin-panel, an internal server-rendered admin tool, choosing the authentication state strategy that best matches the current codebase and roadmap.
question: Select the authentication state strategy that best matches the admin-panel's current architecture (stdlib-only Python HTTP server, server-rendered, single origin) and its known roadmap.
known_constraints: The app is server-rendered by its own web server and served from a single origin (README.md:3-6).
There are no external API consumers today (README.md:4-5).
The product roadmap mentions a possible mobile app, but nothing has been decided (README.md:5-6).
The codebase is a minimal Python stdlib-only app with no dependency manifests (app.py:1-3; no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or package.json in the repository).
No authentication exists yet: the sign-in form is a placeholder with no /login handler and no session or token logic (app.py:5-12).
The development entrypoint binds to 127.0.0.1:8080 over plain HTTP with no TLS configuration (app.py:15-16).
evidence: README.md:3-6 states the app is 'An internal admin panel for a five-person team', is 'server-rendered by its own web server and served from a single origin', has 'no external API consumers today', and its roadmap 'mentions a possible mobile app, but nothing has been decided'.
app.py:1-3 states the app is a 'Minimal server-rendered admin panel (stdlib only)' built on http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler and HTTPServer.
app.py:5-12 contains no authentication logic: a placeholder sign-in form pointing at /login with no handler, no cookies, no sessions, and no tokens.
A repository file inventory shows only README.md and app.py: there is no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or package.json, so a JWT or session library would be a new dependency.
app.py:15-16 binds HTTPServer to 127.0.0.1:8080 with no TLS configuration in the development entrypoint.

alternatives.name: Server-side session with HttpOnly cookie
alternatives.description: Issue an opaque random session ID in an HttpOnly cookie and keep the session record (user, expiry) in a server-side store.
advantages: The session ID is opaque and HttpOnly, so JavaScript on the page cannot read it.
Logout and revocation are immediate: delete the server-side record.
Cookies are sent automatically on same-origin navigation, so plain server-rendered pages work without client-side JavaScript changes.
Achievable with the standard library alone (secrets for ID generation, an in-memory dict or sqlite3 for the store).
disadvantages: Introduces server-side state that must be stored and cleaned up; an in-memory store loses sessions on restart.
Cookie-based auth needs CSRF mitigations (SameSite attribute plus a CSRF token) on state-changing requests.
Non-browser clients cannot rely on cookies and would need a separate token flow if a mobile app is built.
assumptions: An in-process or sqlite session store on the same server is acceptable for a five-person team.
Requests remain same-origin, so SameSite cookie settings are sufficient CSRF mitigation.

alternatives.name: Stateless JWT with Bearer header
alternatives.description: Sign a stateless JWT with an expiry claim, keep it in browser localStorage, and send it as an Authorization: Bearer header on each request.
advantages: Verification is stateless: the server checks only the signature and expiry, so no session store is needed.
Works uniformly for any client that can set an HTTP header, including a future mobile app.
The browser does not send the token automatically, so requests are not exposed to CSRF.
disadvantages: The token is readable by JavaScript, so any XSS vulnerability exposes it until expiry.
Logout and immediate revocation are not possible without a server-side denylist, which removes the statelessness benefit.
A server-rendered app cannot attach Authorization headers on plain navigation, so every protected page load needs custom JavaScript fetch handling.
assumptions: The team is willing to implement JWT sign/verify with hmac/hashlib or to add a dependency.
Exposure of a stolen token until expiry is an acceptable risk for an internal five-person panel.

alternatives.name: Stateless JWT in an HttpOnly cookie
alternatives.description: Sign a stateless JWT with an expiry claim, deliver it in an HttpOnly SameSite cookie, and verify the signature on each request without a session store.
advantages: Verification is stateless, so no session store is required.
HttpOnly cookies are not readable by JavaScript, so XSS cannot read the token itself.
Cookies are sent automatically on same-origin navigation, so plain server-rendered pages work without client-side JavaScript changes.
disadvantages: Like any cookie-based scheme it needs CSRF mitigations (SameSite attribute plus a CSRF token).
Logout and immediate revocation are not possible without a denylist, which removes the statelessness benefit.
Non-browser clients must manage the cookie jar themselves, which is possible but less conventional.
assumptions: The team is willing to implement JWT sign/verify with hmac/hashlib or to add a dependency.
A short token lifetime is acceptable for admin sessions, or a denylist can be added later if revocation is needed.

criteria.name: Fit for a single-origin server-rendered app
rubric: Awkward for same-origin server-rendered navigation and needs extra client plumbing
Workable but adds client-side or cross-origin complexity
Natural fit: works with plain same-origin server-rendered navigation

criteria.name: Implementation effort on the stdlib-only codebase
rubric: Needs new dependencies or significant infrastructure
Requires moderate new code with no new dependencies
Achievable with a small amount of stdlib-only code

criteria.name: Immediate logout and revocation
rubric: Access stays valid until token expiry; no immediate revocation
Immediate revocation requires adding a denylist
Immediate revocation is direct: delete the server-side record

criteria.name: Exposure to XSS token theft and CSRF
rubric: Exposed to both XSS token theft and CSRF
Exposed to XSS token theft or CSRF, but not both

criteria.name: Readiness for a future non-browser client (mobile app)
rubric: Requires a separate flow or rework for non-browser clients
Works for browser and non-browser clients with no changes

criteria.name: Server-side state and operational complexity
rubric: Requires durable shared state or an external store
Adds in-process state that is lost on restart
